implementation_notes: The JDK's own descriptor: javax.security.auth.Subject groups the identities (java.security.Principal instances) and credentials of the authenticated entity, and getPrincipals() / getPrincipals(Class) are the accessors consumers use; credentials stay in the Subject's credential sets and never leave the authentication code. Propagation moved on - Subject.doAs and getSubject are deprecated for removal, so bind the Subject with Subject.callAs(...) or read it with Subject.current() (JDK 18+) and pass it explicitly to the code that decides. Choose this variant for plain Java SE or an app server that already exposes a caller principal; prefer the framework variants when Spring or Jakarta EE is already in the stack.
pitfalls: Subject.getPrincipals() returns the live internal set while getPrincipals(Class) returns a fresh copy - mutating the first changes the subject, mutating the second silently does nothing.
A Subject may hold several Principals, so there is no single "the user": relying on getName() from an arbitrary principal makes the identity ambiguous - use a typed principal class.
doAs/getSubject are deprecated for removal and now fail when the security manager is disallowed (JDK 24+); new code must use callAs/current instead.

variants.name: Spring Security Authentication in the SecurityContext
variants.implementation_notes: In Spring the descriptor is the Authentication stored in the SecurityContext: consumers call SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication() and read getPrincipal()/getAuthorities(), or let the framework resolve a typed principal into controller parameters with @AuthenticationPrincipal. The descriptor contract is the framework's, and the principal object is whatever the AuthenticationProvider put there, so define a typed principal (a UserDetails implementation) instead of casting strings at every site. Choose this variant when Spring Security already owns the filter chain; it is the least code in a Spring application.
pitfalls: SecurityContextHolder is thread-bound by default and does not follow work onto @Async or Reactor threads - the identity disappears unless the context is explicitly propagated.
getPrincipal() is typed Object: casting it in every consumer throws ClassCastException for anonymous or pre-authenticated tokens, so resolve a typed principal once.
Calling SecurityContextHolder.setContext() outside the filter chain leaks a principal across requests on pooled threads.

variants.name: Jakarta Security SecurityContext (container-managed caller)
variants.implementation_notes: The Jakarta EE standard API: inject SecurityContext and ask getCallerPrincipal() (a java.security.Principal supplied by the container), getPrincipalsByType(Class), isCallerInRole(...) or getAllDeclaredCallerRoles(). The container performs authentication (for example through an HttpAuthenticationMechanism) and the application only reads caller data, which realizes the pattern as one standard interface across Servlet, EJB, REST, CDI and WebSocket components. Choose it when the runtime is a Jakarta EE container and portability across implementations matters more than the framework-specific ergonomics of the Spring variant.
pitfalls: getCallerPrincipal() returns null for unauthenticated callers - guards must fail closed on null rather than compare names.

The container principal and an application principal can be different objects: the spec requires the same getName(), so compare by name and use getPrincipalsByType(...) for the application's own type.
Jakarta Security reports the container's authentication result only; identities established by an application-owned token filter are invisible to it.
